passage: Daycare note, Monday. At tidy-up time Veer (2) crouched behind the curtain, but his feet and bottom stuck out. When I called, "Where's Veer?" he pressed his hands over his eyes and giggled, sure he was hidden. Later he held up his drawing to show me, with the picture facing his own nose. I saw only the blank back. I turned it round and said, "Now I can see it!" He looked puzzled, then turned it back to himself. — Aparna

qa.q: What stuck out from behind the curtain?
qa.a: Veer's feet and bottom.

qa.q: Why did Veer giggle with his hands over his eyes?
qa.a: Veer felt delighted and sure he was hidden, believing that because he couldn't see anyone, nobody could see him.

qa.q: What did Aparna do to help Veer notice another view, and what could Aparna keep doing?
qa.a: Aparna turned the drawing round and said "Now I can see it!", and can keep playing such games so he slowly learns others see differently.

qa.q: What does Aparna see that Veer can't yet imagine?
qa.a: Aparna sees his feet sticking out and the blank back of his drawing, while Veer assumes everyone sees what he sees.

grounding: A caregiver notes a toddler who covers his eyes to hide and shows a picture facing himself, unable to imagine another view.

passage: In the courtyard of their house near Kottayam, Tomy, two, heard his mother, Elizabeth, calling him for his bath. He squeezed his eyes shut and stood very still beside the coconut pile. "Tomy gone," he announced. His sister Anjali laughed. "I can see you!" Tomy shut his eyes tighter. Then he held up a shell to show Anjali, the shiny side toward his own face. "See? Pretty!" Anjali saw only its rough grey back.

qa.q: What did Tomy announce with his eyes shut?
qa.a: "Tomy gone."

qa.q: Why did Tomy shut his eyes tighter when Anjali said she could see him?
qa.a: Tomy felt determined to stay hidden; to him hiding meant not seeing, so squeezing his eyes harder seemed like hiding better.

qa.q: How could Anjali gently show Tomy what she sees?
qa.a: She could turn the shell round toward herself and say "Now I see the shiny side!", making a simple game of it.

qa.q: What is it like for Anjali when Tomy shows her the shell?
qa.a: She is shown only a rough grey back while Tomy is sure she sees the pretty side, which is funny and a little puzzling for her.

grounding: A toddler shuts his eyes to hide and shows a shell facing himself, not yet imagining that others see differently.

passage: Rain was pouring and the auto meter was ticking outside the preschool gate when Nikita reached Gautam, four. He grabbed her hand. "Mummy, the big one fell and Riya cried and Ma'am got the thing!" "Which big one? What thing?" she asked, fighting with the umbrella. Gautam frowned, as if she were being silly. "The one! You know!" In the auto he pressed his face to the window. "You're sad too, because the swings are wet," he said. Nikita, who had not thought about swings all day, squeezed his hand. "Tell me slowly. What fell first?"

qa.q: Who cried, according to Gautam?
qa.a: Riya.

qa.q: Why did Gautam frown when Nikita asked "Which big one?"
qa.a: He assumed she already knew what he had seen at school, so her question seemed silly to him.

qa.q: What did Nikita try, and why does it suit a four-year-old?
qa.a: She asked him to tell it slowly and start with what fell first, which helps him fill in the story step by step.

qa.q: What is it like for Nikita trying to follow the story in the rain?
qa.a: It's confusing and a bit stressful, with the meter ticking and the umbrella fighting her, yet she stays patient.

grounding: A preschool boy tells his mother a half-story assuming she knows what he saw, and assumes she shares his feelings about the swings.

passage: In their Pune flat, Yuvraj, five, burst in from school. "Mummy, Bittu did it again and then the fish!" Sharmila put down her tea. "Who's Bittu? What fish?" Yuvraj stamped his foot. "Bittu, Mummy! You know!" His Minakshi Masi, visiting, tried: "Was the fish in a tank?" "Obviously." Then he held out his chocolate to Masi. "You want it. Everybody loves orange ones." Masi, who disliked orange chocolates, took a tiny bite and smiled. Sharmila sat down beside him. "Start from the bus. What happened first?"

qa.q: What flavour of chocolate did Yuvraj offer Masi?
qa.a: An orange one.

qa.q: Why did Yuvraj stamp his foot when Sharmila asked who Bittu was?
qa.a: He believed his mother already knew Bittu and the fish, so her question felt frustrating to him.

qa.q: What small step did Sharmila take to help Yuvraj tell the story?
qa.a: She sat beside him and asked him to start from the bus, giving him a simple order to follow.

qa.q: How might Minakshi Masi feel about the orange chocolate?
qa.a: Masi doesn't like orange ones but took a tiny bite to be kind, seeing that Yuvraj assumed everyone shares his taste.

grounding: A preschool boy gives puzzling half-stories, assuming his mother knows what he saw, and thinks everyone likes what he likes.

passage: At the anganwadi in a village near Sagar, Siddharth, five, snatched the only toy tractor from Pradeep, whose face crumpled into a howl. Sunita didi, the anganwadi worker, didn't scold. She knelt and held up a picture card of a crying child. "Look at this face. What happened, do you think?" "Someone took the thing," Siddharth said. "And how is Pradeep's face now?" Siddharth looked. "Same." Sunita didi picked up two cloth dolls. "Let's play. This doll had the tractor. What does it say?" Siddharth made the doll say, "Give back!" Then he slowly held out the tractor.

qa.q: What did Sunita didi hold up after Siddharth snatched the tractor?
qa.a: A picture card of a crying child.

qa.q: What did Siddharth seem to realise when he said Pradeep's face was "Same"?
qa.a: He was beginning to see that Pradeep felt like the child in the picture, upset because something was taken.

qa.q: Why did the doll game work better than a scolding?
qa.a: Speaking for the doll let Siddharth feel what Pradeep felt, so he chose to give the tractor back himself.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when Siddharth held out the tractor?
qa.a: Pradeep would likely feel relieved and cared for, seeing that the other child noticed the hurt.

grounding: A caregiver uses a picture card and pretend play to help a child see how another child feels.

passage: At a playgroup in Cape Town, Lucia, four, laughed when Thabo's sandcastle collapsed. Thabo's lip wobbled. Their teacher, Mrs Dlamini, sat down in the sand. "Lucia, when my tower falls down, I feel sad inside. How do you think Thabo feels?" Lucia shrugged. "It's funny." Mrs Dlamini held up a small plastic figure. "This is Thabo. His castle just fell. Can you make him talk?" Lucia took it and said in a tiny voice, "My castle is broken." She stopped smiling. "Thabo, want help?" she asked, and began patting the sand.

qa.q: What happened to Thabo's sandcastle?
qa.a: It collapsed.

qa.q: What changed in Lucia's mind while she made the figure talk?
qa.a: Speaking as Thabo let her feel his sadness, so the fall stopped seeming funny and she wanted to help.

qa.q: Which of Mrs Dlamini's moves helped most, and why?
qa.a: Sharing her own feeling first and then using the figure for pretend play, which showed Lucia how to imagine Thabo's side.

qa.q: How might Thabo feel when Lucia offers to help?
qa.a: Thabo would likely feel comforted, since the child who laughed now sees his disappointment and wants to rebuild with him.

grounding: A teacher models naming her own feelings and uses pretend play to help a young child take another child's view.

passage: Only forty minutes before the Jayanagar library closed, and Mridul, ten, and Sumit still hadn't picked a book for their project. "You want the planets one, I know," Mridul said. "You think dinosaurs are for babies. Fine, planets." He felt proud; last year he'd have just grabbed dinosaurs. Then Sumit said, "For the next project, I'm pairing with Farhan. He's good at drawing." Mridul's face went hot. "So you think I'm useless." "I didn't say that." "You meant it." Mridul stomped to the checkout. The lights flicked, the guard called closing time, and Sumit stood holding the planets book, looking confused.

qa.q: How long was it before the library closed?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Mridul decide Sumit thought he was useless?
qa.a: His hurt at not being picked for the next project was so strong that he read his own feeling into Sumit's words.

qa.q: What could Mridul try the next time a hot feeling like that comes?
qa.a: He could pause and ask Sumit what was meant, the same way he had guessed Sumit's wish for the planets book.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt holding the planets book?
qa.a: Sumit probably felt confused and hurt, since a simple plan about drawing turned into being accused of something never said.

grounding: Under time pressure, a boy correctly reads what a friend wants but misjudges the friend's meaning once his own feelings are hurt.

passage: Hrithik, eleven, was proud of the plan. Pankaj's birthday surprise was set for Saturday in their Kolkata colony hall, and Pankaj had no idea. "He thinks we forgot," Hrithik whispered to the others. "So act normal." On Saturday Pankaj walked in, gasped and laughed. Hrithik handed over his present: a new football, the thing Hrithik wanted most in the world. Pankaj smiled politely. "Thanks... I'll use it." Then his eyes lit up at a book from his cousin. Hrithik's chest went tight. "Everyone loves football," he muttered to his mother at home. "He's just pretending not to." She asked, "Does Pankaj play much?" Hrithik went quiet. "He mostly reads," he admitted, still sulking.

qa.q: Where was Pankaj's surprise held?
qa.a: In their Kolkata colony hall.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik insist that Pankaj was only pretending not to love football?
qa.a: He was disappointed that his gift wasn't loved, and his strong feelings made it hard to accept that Pankaj simply wants different things.

qa.q: What question helped Hrithik think again, and what might he do next time?
qa.a: His mother asking "Does Pankaj play much?"; next time he could think about what Pankaj enjoys before choosing a gift.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt opening the football?
qa.a: Pankaj probably felt grateful for the thought but not excited, and tried to be polite so as not to hurt Hrithik.

grounding: A boy understands his friend doesn't know about a surprise, but struggles to accept the friend wants different things when his own feelings are involved.

passage: "Amma, I'm not going to school tomorrow." "Why, Kartik?" "Everyone saw me drop the trophy on stage. Everyone. They're all talking about it." "Everyone?" "The whole school, Amma. Nobody has ever been this humiliated. Ever." "Aparna, didn't you fall off the stage in Class 9?" "Into the flower pots. In a sari. In front of the chief guest." "Akka, that's different. It's not the same for me." "Kartik, how many people mentioned it today?" "...Two. But they were all thinking it." "Or thinking about their own lunch." "You don't understand." Aparna ruffled his hair. "Maybe not. But I still remember the flower pots, and nobody else does." Kartik almost smiled. "The chief guest, really?" "Front row." Rukmini, their Amma, put a plate of murukku between them.

qa.q: How many people mentioned the trophy to Kartik that day?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: Why is Kartik so sure the whole school is talking about him?
qa.a: He feels that everyone is watching him and that his embarrassment is unlike anyone else's, so two comments seem like the whole school.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation for Kartik?
qa.a: Aparna's flower-pot story and her saying nobody else remembers it, which made him almost smile and see others have felt this too.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel sharing her own embarrassing fall with her brother?
qa.a: She seems warm and a little amused, willing to laugh at herself so that he feels less alone.

grounding: A teenage boy feels his embarrassment is unique and that everyone is watching him, and his sister's story begins to soften that.

passage: Last year, when my best friend Bhavna moved to Delhi, I was sure nobody in the history of the world had felt what I felt. I wrote it in a notebook: "No one understands. No one could." Walking into school, I felt every face turn to check whether I looked sad. I even changed how I walked. Then in December I went to an inter-school science camp in Mysuru. On the second night, sitting on the hostel steps, a boy from Hubli said his closest friend had moved to Dubai, and he'd felt everyone staring at him for weeks. Another boy nodded. I just sat there. My exact feeling, in somebody else's mouth. I'm Kunal, and I still have that notebook. It reads a little differently now. Amma calls it her son's tragic-poet phase.

qa.q: Where was the inter-school science camp?
qa.a: In Mysuru.

qa.q: Why did Kunal change how he walked into school?
qa.a: He felt everyone was watching him to see if he looked sad, and believed his pain was unlike anyone else's.

qa.q: What turning point softened Kunal's belief that no one could understand?
qa.a: Hearing a boy from Hubli describe the same feeling on the hostel steps, which showed others had felt it too.

qa.q: How might the boy from Hubli have felt when Kunal sat there listening?
qa.a: He may have felt less alone too, sharing something private and finding that others nodded in recognition.

grounding: A teenage boy looks back on feeling that nobody had ever felt his loss and everyone was watching him, until meeting others softened it.

passage:
Friday night
Tanuja came home and slammed her bag down. A pimple, the day before the dance. "Everyone will stare at it the whole time. Nobody has ever had one this bad, Amma. You don't understand." My first thought was, nobody is looking at your chin, beta. I bit it back. Fifteen is like this; I remember it. I just said, "That sounds really stressful." She talked for twenty minutes, and I mostly listened.
Later, over dinner, I asked what Riya was nervous about. She paused. "Riya's scared she'll forget the steps. She practised all week." A little silence. "Hm. I didn't even ask her." Small step, but a real one. I'll keep asking about others, slowly, without lecturing. She took the concealer to school and a cup of chai to her room. Good enough.
— Nikita

qa.q: What was Riya scared about before the dance?
qa.a: That she would forget the steps.

qa.q: What did Nikita feel like saying, and why did she hold it back?
qa.a: Nikita felt a little impatient and wanted to say nobody would look at Tanuja's chin, but held back because she saw this self-focus as normal at fifteen and wanted Tanuja to feel heard.

qa.q: Which of Nikita's choices gently widened Tanuja's view?
qa.a: Asking at dinner what Riya was nervous about, which led Tanuja to notice she hadn't asked her friend.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt when her mother simply said it sounded stressful?
qa.a: Tanuja likely felt listened to rather than dismissed, which is why she kept talking for twenty minutes.

grounding: A mother's diary shows her treating her teen daughter's self-focus as a normal stage, listening first and slowly widening her view.

passage: At Vinita aunty's flat next door in Lucknow, Rafiq, five, was carrying her blue cup to the sink when it bumped the tap. A thin crack ran down its side, and milk dripped on the floor. Vinita aunty came in. Rafiq put the cup behind his back. "It's not cracked." "Can I see?" "It was always like that." He stood on the milk puddle with his sock. "I didn't spill." His eyes stayed fixed on her face. Vinita aunty knelt down. "Rafiq, cups crack. I'm not angry. Let's wipe it together." His shoulders dropped. "It bumped," he whispered.

qa.q: What did the cup bump into?
qa.a: The tap.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq say the cup was always like that?
qa.a: He was afraid of getting into trouble, so pretending the crack wasn't there felt safer than saying what happened.

qa.q: Which words from Vinita aunty helped Rafiq tell the truth, and why?
qa.a: "Cups crack. I'm not angry. Let's wipe it together" took away his fear of trouble, so he could admit it bumped.

qa.q: How might Vinita aunty feel seeing Rafiq stand on the milk with his sock?
qa.a: She might feel a mix of amusement and tenderness, understanding he was scared rather than trying to trick her.

grounding: A young child insists a cracked cup was never cracked and denies spilling, because fear of trouble outweighs accuracy.

passage: "Ojas, why is there juice on the sofa?" "There's no juice, Papa." "This orange patch here?" "It was already there." "Your glass is empty." "I drank it." "All of it went in your mouth?" "Yes. I didn't spill anything." "Ojas, look at me. Are you worried I'll be angry?" Ojas stared at his socks. "...Yes." "I won't be. Spills happen. I spilled tea on this same sofa last month." "You did?" "Ask Amma. Now, shall we get the cloth together?" "It was a small spill." "I know. Small spills are easy to clean." Harish handed him the cloth. Ojas scrubbed very hard.

qa.q: Where was the orange patch?
qa.a: On the sofa.

qa.q: What was Ojas worried about when he said "I didn't spill anything"?
qa.a: He was worried Papa would be angry, and that fear felt bigger than telling what happened.

qa.q: What was the turning point that helped Ojas admit the spill?
qa.a: Papa asking if he was worried and saying he wouldn't be angry, even sharing his own tea spill, so Ojas felt safe.

qa.q: How might Harish feel watching Ojas scrub very hard?
qa.a: Harish might feel tender and a bit amused, seeing that Ojas wants to make things right once the fear is gone.

grounding: A young child denies a spill in front of the evidence because fear of trouble outweighs wanting to be accurate.

passage: Class teacher's note, Class 5A. Ojas (10) has been saying "Everything's fine, Ma'am" several times a day, even when nobody asked. His mother told me last week that his father lost his job a month ago. Since then Ojas has stopped asking questions in class, which is unusual for him. He yawns through first period and says he "just reads late." On Tuesday he snapped at his partner over a ruler and tore his own worksheet. When I asked gently how home was, he said quickly, "Papa is just resting. It's fine." I didn't push. I kept his routine steady and let him help in the library at lunch, where he relaxed. I called his mother to suggest simple, honest words at home, and asked our school counsellor to check in with him this week. — Trisha

qa.q: What did Ojas tear on Tuesday?
qa.a: His own worksheet.

qa.q: Why might Ojas keep saying "Everything's fine" when nobody asked?
qa.a: Not knowing or not talking about his father's job loss seems to feel safer than facing the worry, though the tension still shows.

qa.q: Which of Trisha's steps seems most helpful, and why?
qa.a: Keeping his routine steady and asking the counsellor to check in, while encouraging honest words at home, so he has support without being pushed.

qa.q: How might Ojas's partner have felt when Ojas snapped over the ruler?
qa.a: The partner was probably surprised and hurt, not knowing the snap came from worry about home.

grounding: A teacher notices a boy who says everything is fine after his father's job loss, while poor sleep and short temper show the strain.

passage:
Thursday
Mummy's office closed. That's all I know and I don't want to know more. When Kashish asked at the bus stop, I said, "Everything's fine, she's just taking a holiday." Mummy tried to talk to me after dinner. "Beti, come sit." I said I had homework and went to my room. If I don't ask, maybe it's not real.
But I couldn't sleep again. I lay there listening to the fan and to Papa and Mummy talking quietly in the kitchen. This morning I shouted at Kashish for taking my pencil, and it wasn't even my good pencil. She looked so hurt.
I'm not scared. I'm just tired.
Maybe tomorrow I'll ask Mummy one question. Just one. Like, will we still go to Nani's in May.
— Avni

qa.q: What did Avni tell Kashish at the bus stop?
qa.a: "Everything's fine, she's just taking a holiday."

qa.q: Why did Avni say she had homework when Mummy tried to talk?
qa.a: Not knowing felt safer than hearing worrying news, so she avoided the conversation even though the worry was still there.

qa.q: What small step is Avni thinking of, and why could it help?
qa.a: Asking Mummy one simple question, like whether they'll still go to Nani's, which lets her face the news a little at a time.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt when Avni shouted about the pencil?
qa.a: Kashish looked hurt, and probably confused, since it wasn't even Avni's good pencil and she didn't know about the worry at home.

grounding: A child's diary shows her insisting all is fine after her mother's job loss, while poor sleep and snapping show the tension.

subtype: Facing a bad result in small doses [Response]
passage: For three days after the half-yearly results in their village near Bikaner, Sarita, fifteen, told everyone the maths marks weren't out yet. The report card sat folded in the wheat bin under the stairs. Twenty-eight out of eighty. Each night her stomach knotted. On the fourth evening, on the rooftop, her cousin Himani didi was folding clothes. Sarita's mouth felt dry. "Didi. I got twenty-eight in maths." Saying it out loud made her chest shake, and then, oddly, loosen. Himani didi put down the clothes. "Okay. Thank you for telling me." She didn't scold. They sat on the parapet and made a small plan: ask Masterji for the paper tomorrow, one chapter a day, and tell Amma on Sunday together. Sarita took the report card out of the wheat bin that night.

qa.q: Where did Sarita hide the report card?
qa.a: In the wheat bin under the stairs.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel just after saying her mark out loud?
qa.a: Her chest shook, then oddly loosened, as if saying it to one trusted person took some weight off.

qa.q: What made Sarita's way of facing the result work?
qa.a: She told one trusted person first, then made a small plan and chose when to tell Amma, so she could act instead of hiding.

qa.q: How might Himani didi feel being the first to hear?
qa.a: Himani didi seemed glad to be trusted and calm, choosing to thank Sarita and help plan rather than scold.

grounding: A teenager who hid a poor result tells one trusted person first and then makes a plan, facing it in small doses.

subtype: Facing a bad result in small doses [Response]
passage: Camila, sixteen, didn't open the school portal for three days after the chemistry grades went up in Madrid. "It'll be fine," she told herself, scrolling videos until midnight. On Thursday, in the library, she finally clicked. A three out of ten. She shut the laptop so fast it banged. For an hour she did nothing. Then she texted Nour, the one friend who never made a joke of things: "I got a 3 in chemistry." Nour replied within a minute: "Thank you for telling me. Want to talk after class?" They sat on the wall outside the school. Saying it again, out loud, felt less heavy. Together they wrote three lines in her notebook: see Señora Ruiz on Monday, redo the test questions, tell Papá on Sunday at lunch.

qa.q: What grade did Camila get in chemistry?
qa.a: A three out of ten.

qa.q: Why did Camila avoid the portal for three days?
qa.a: Not looking softened the shock and kept her dread away, even though it couldn't change the result.

qa.q: Which choice helped Camila move from avoiding to acting?
qa.a: Texting one trusted friend, Nour, and then writing a short plan of three steps together.

qa.q: How might Nour have felt receiving Camila's text?
qa.a: Nour probably felt trusted and wanted to help, replying quickly and kindly instead of making a joke.

grounding: A teenager who avoided a bad grade says it first to one trusted friend and then plans, accepting it in small doses.

passage: In the girls' hostel of the small college in Hassan, Indu, nineteen, had tucked the counsellor's letter inside her economics book, unopened. Her internal marks had slid from sixties to thirties. The hostel fee slip was two months old. "It'll sort itself out," she told her roommate Payal, and went to the temple fair with the juniors every evening that week, laughing a little too loudly. Payal noticed she'd stopped studying at night and slept badly. On Monday morning a notice went up outside the office: students with unpaid fees would not get exam hall tickets after Wednesday. Indu's name was on it. She stood staring for a long time. Then she went back to the room, opened the economics book, and read the counsellor's letter for the first time. "Payal," she said quietly, "will you come with me?"

qa.q: Where had Indu tucked the counsellor's letter?
qa.a: Inside her economics book, unopened.

qa.q: Why did Indu go to the temple fair every evening and laugh a little too loudly?
qa.a: Keeping busy and cheerful helped her push away the dread about her marks and fees, so she didn't have to look at them.

qa.q: What forced Indu to act, and what could have helped earlier?
qa.a: The notice with her name forced her; reading the counsellor's letter when it came, or telling Payal sooner, could have helped before it became urgent.

qa.q: How might Payal have seen Indu during that week?
qa.a: Payal noticed the stopped studying and poor sleep, and was probably worried but unsure how to help until Indu asked.

grounding: A student ignores falling marks, unpaid fees and a counsellor's letter until a deadline forces her to face them.
